**EPC launches initiative to standardise EUDI wallet acceptance for payments**

*A consistent rulebook for accepting EU Digital Identity Wallets could prevent fragmented adoption across the bloc, addressing a gap that payment service providers have lacked until now.*

The European Payments Council (EPC) has approved work on a standardisation initiative designed to ensure payment service providers accept EU Digital Identity wallets in a consistent way. The framework, known as SCARLET, will define how wallets interact with payment processes, covering both in-store and online use cases.

EU Digital Identity wallets are a cornerstone of the EU's digital identity regulation, but their integration with payments infrastructure has lacked a common technical and operational standard. Without one, there is a risk that wallet acceptance fragments along national or scheme-specific lines, replicating the interoperability problems the EU has spent years trying to resolve in payments. SCARLET is the EPC's attempt to pre-empt that outcome by establishing shared rules before wallets reach mass deployment.

The initiative sits alongside the EPC's existing instant payments and SEPA rulebooks and signals the body's expanding remit beyond traditional payment instruments. For banks and payment processors already preparing for PSD3 and the instant payments regulation, EU Digital Identity wallet readiness is becoming another compliance and product development workstream that requires early attention.

*Sources: [EPC to create EU Digital Identity Wallet framework for PSPs](https://www.finextra.com/newsarticle/48606/epc-to-create-eu-digital-identity-wallet-framework-for-psps?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra | [EPC Launches SCARLET to Standardise EU Digital Identity Wallet Acceptance for Payments](https://ffnews.com/news/european-payments-council-launches-scarlet-initiative-on-eu-digital-identity-wal-2ae0f323) — Ffnews*

**Euronet and Fireblocks extend partnership to stablecoin-funded card issuing**

*The deal brings stablecoin balances into the card issuing process, testing whether existing payments infrastructure can absorb digital asset funding without requiring new merchant acceptance.*

Euronet, the payments infrastructure group, is extending its partnership with digital asset platform Fireblocks to enable stablecoin-funded card issuing. The arrangement allows card programmes to draw on stablecoin balances at the point of issuance, converting to fiat for settlement through existing card networks.

Stablecoins are increasingly connecting to conventional payment rails. Mastercard integrated BVNK for fiat-stablecoin settlement earlier this month, and Visa has partnered with Mesh to make crypto balances spendable across its network. Euronet operates as a processor and infrastructure provider rather than a scheme or fintech; its entry into stablecoin-funded issuing suggests the plumbing layer of European payments is beginning to accommodate stablecoin flows, not just the consumer-facing layer.

Whether stablecoin-funded cards can operate within MiCA's e-money token framework and meet the settlement finality requirements that card schemes impose remains an open question for issuers. Euronet's infrastructure spans ATM networks, money transfers and merchant acquiring across Europe, giving the partnership a broader potential footprint than a standalone fintech experiment.

*Sources: [Euronet and Fireblocks team on stablecoin-funded card issuing](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111344/euronet-and-fireblocks-team-on-stablecoin-funded-card-issuing?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**FCA outlines regulatory framework for agentic finance and AI-driven payments**

*Plans to address agent identity, delegated authority and accountability signal that UK regulation is preparing to catch up with the rapid deployment of AI agents across payments and investment services.*

Jessica Rusu, the Financial Conduct Authority's chief data, information and intelligence officer, used a speech at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series on October 19 to announce that the regulator will develop a framework for agentic finance covering agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution. The FCA will work with industry, other regulators and frontier AI labs to build the approach, which responds to the growing number of AI agents capable of initiating payments, managing investments and transacting with other agents on consumers' behalf.

Alongside the framework announcement, the FCA published examples of good and poor AI practice across financial services. Good practice included chatbots that flagged potentially vulnerable customers to human advisers and independent ethics panels reviewing AI tools before deployment. Poor practice included firms introducing AI without a clear need, excluding vulnerable consumers and launching automated customer journeys without sufficient testing. Rusu said the regulator expects senior managers to be personally accountable for AI systems deployed in their areas, describing the retrofitting of governance after deployment as "the wrong way around".

The speech also disclosed that 86% of financial firms now use AI, citing a forthcoming joint FCA and Bank of England survey, and that only 40% of consumers correctly understand they have no recourse when acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. For payments firms, the agentic finance framework is the element to watch: it will shape the rules under which the AI-initiated transactions that Visa, Mastercard and several European banks have piloted this year will ultimately operate in the UK market.

*Sources: [UK's FCA Plans Regulatory Framework for Agentic Finance](https://www.pymnts.com/news/artificial-intelligence/2026/united-kingdom-financial-conduct-authority-plans-regulatory-framework-agentic-finance/) — PYMNTS*

**Prism Data raises $20m for open banking credit analytics in the US**

*Transaction-based risk scoring that works across aggregators offers a cross-border comparison point as European open finance moves toward cashflow-based lending.*

Prism Data, a US-based open banking analytics firm led by CEO Jason Rosen, has raised $20 million in Series A funding. The company provides transaction analytics software that generates proprietary risk scores from open banking data, designed to be compatible with data from any aggregator as well as banks' own deposit account records and PDF statements.

The round comes as cashflow-based underwriting gains traction on both sides of the Atlantic. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority has signalled that open banking data will reshape mortgage affordability checks, and Experian launched a consumer reporting agency for cashflow-based underwriting earlier this year. Prism's aggregator-agnostic approach addresses a practical problem: lenders working across multiple data sources need scoring models that normalise transaction data regardless of its origin.

Prism's model offers a reference point as PSD3 and the Financial Data Access regulation expand the scope of data available to third parties in Europe. The challenge of turning raw transaction data into reliable, standardised credit signals is not unique to the US market and will intensify as open finance widens beyond payments accounts.

*Sources: [Prism Data Tecnologies Raises $20M in Series A Funding](https://www.finsmes.com/2026/10/prism-data-tecnologies-raises-20m-in-series-a-funding.html) — FinSMEs | [Prism Data raises $20m](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111338/prism-data-raises-20m) — Finextra Research*
